outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your poem, refined for clarity and lyrical flow while preserving its imagery, structure, and emotional core:

---

**Insomnia, With Ghosts**

I wish I could be
a ship that carries
its beloved captain
through the night—
sleeping through every storm,
slipping past dawn,
waking to nothing
but strange, unlived things
to report.

Instead I rise
in the dark
and parachute
quietly down
to the kitchen,
performing that purely mental ritual:
switching on
the useless machine of worry.

Above me, she sleeps
like the innocent,
still dreaming—
elder sister
to all gentle things.

The white screen
asks, impassive,
what doesn't matter
until it does.
So I shut it down
and think instead
of the lake near where I live.

It's a lagoon,
brightening now
like an old television
just switched on—
a Zenith, maybe—
its two arms stretching
without feeling
eastward, to embrace
an empty park.

A little light,
and suddenly
everything casts a shadow.
I almost hear
a silent bell,
low voices.

I brought us
to this old city,
where the port still connects
to the wider world,
where everyone pretends to know
they're living on an island,
waiting for the great wave—
in whatever form it takes,
radiation perhaps.

In the yard,
the wind moves,
and the whole black sky
looks down, if only for an instant,
through my drowsy,
solitary frame.

A complicated child—
a hologram—flickers,
clutching a green plastic shovel,
angry,
then vanishes,
leaving behind
an empty column, waiting.

Bill, who I knew
carried such anger,
is dead now.
Whatever he was going through,
I kept my distance.
I never did a thing.

I loved his poems—
he was truly gifted.
I keep forgetting his last name,
yet I always leave
his handmade book
on my desk—

not to remember,
but because for hours afterward,
everything everyone says
sounds like a language
I never knew,
but somehow now speak.

Spirit, I know
you would have hated
how I think,
though you might have liked
this music
playing in another room,
pushing that alien voice
into the millennium
you left too soon.

Spirit,
you were right—
all noble things are gone,
except this: to struggle,
and to be loved.

---

**Insomnia at the Lagoon**

I wanted only to sleep the way a ship
carries its captain through the night—
unconscious, trusting, borne along
by something larger than my own small will.
Instead I woke at three, at four, the dark
pressing its palm against the window glass,
and lay there turning thoughts like stones
I could not skip across any water,
each one sinking, each one dragging down
another thought behind it.

By five the lagoon had begun to lighten,
gray easing into pewter, into pearl.
I watched from the sill, half-dressed, half-real,
a spectator to my own quiet street—
the gulls not yet awake, the water
holding its breath before the first boat's wake.
Somewhere behind me in the house
my family slept the sleep of the untroubled,
innocent in their ignorance of the hour,
while I kept vigil with the brightening air,
apart from them, apart from everything,
a man watching the world through glass.

This city is old, built on water and patience,
its stones softened by five centuries of tides.
And yet I think we live here each an island,
close enough to wave, too far to touch—
each house its own small isolated watch,
each window holding someone else
who cannot sleep, who waits as I wait
for something none of us can name,
some flood, some fire, some quiet catastrophe
we sense but cannot see approaching,
the way animals grow still before a storm.

I think of Bill tonight, dead now three years,
who wrote lines sharper than any I could manage,
who burned through friendships like cheap matches,
angry at the end, and mostly alone—
alone by choice, or loneliness by then
too old a habit to be broken.
I kept my distance too. I told myself
I was protecting something—my own peace,
my own uncomplicated hours—
and let him drift off toward whatever door
he finally walked through without me.
Now I cannot even hold his last name
steady in my mind; it slips like water
through fingers that once might have reached for him.

Bill, wherever you are, if you are anywhere,
forgive the distance I kept and keep,
forgive a memory grown careless with your name.
The noble things are gone, or going—
courage, certainty, the old religious comforts
that once made dying seem like sleep.
What's left to us is smaller, harder-won:
the daily struggle to keep loving anyway,
to reach across the water toward each other
though the lagoon stays gray, though morning comes
no easier than any of the nights before it.
This is what I have to offer you—
not peace, but the attempt at peace,
not sleep, but the willingness to wake
and try again to love what still remains.

# Insomnia's Kitchen

Three in the morning and the bed
has become an accusation, its sheets
twisted into the shape of every question
I cannot answer lying down. So I rise,
padding past the room where sleep
still pretends to live, into the kitchen
where the linoleum holds the day's
last warmth like a secret.

I fill the kettle not because I want tea
but because the sound of water
approaching boil is a kind of company.
I sit at the table in this small circle
of lamplight, and let the machine begin—
that quiet engine of worry
that never needs fuel, only darkness
and an idle mind to turn its gears.

I had imagined, climbing into bed,
some voyage of untroubled sleep,
a ship gliding through calm black water,
no cargo but rest, no destination
but morning. Instead I am anchored here,
watching thoughts drift past like debris:
old arguments, replayed and revised,
the bills not paid, the calls not returned,
and always, eventually, Bill himself—

dead three years now, and still
he pulls up a chair across from me
in memory's insistent way, still laughing
at some joke whose punchline
I can no longer recall, only the shape
of his laughter, the gap in his teeth,
the way he'd tilt his head back
like he was drinking the sound of his own joy.

I talk to him sometimes, here,
in this kitchen that holds no one
but functions like a confessional
for a faith I'm not sure I keep.
The words come out wrong, always—
language failing the way it always fails
when the freight is too heavy,
when what I mean is larger
than any sentence I can build to hold it.

Isolation is this: the space between
what I feel and what I can say,
the distance from my chest
to my own mouth. Some nights
it seems unbridgeable. The worry machine
knows this, feeds on this, whispers
that connection is a lie we tell ourselves,
that we are each of us alone
in our separate kitchens, drinking
our separate teas, mourning
our separate dead.

But the kettle whistles, and I rise
to quiet it, and in that small act—
crossing the floor, turning off the flame—
something shifts. The noble things fade, yes.
The certainties I held at twenty
have thinned like hair, like patience,
like the belief that meaning
arrives in grand, unmistakable forms.

What's left isn't nothing, though.
What's left is this: the struggle
to speak anyway, imperfectly,
to a friend who is or isn't there.
The willingness to sit with worry
rather than pretend it absent.
And underneath it all, still burning
like a pilot light in a dark house—

the capacity to be loved. Not the guarantee.
Not even, some nights, the evidence.
Just the capacity, intact,
like a room kept ready
though no guest has come in years.

I take my tea back to the window,
watch the dark begin its slow surrender
to a gray that isn't quite morning
but promises it, the way a friend's voice
promises understanding
even when the words come out wrong.

This is enough. This has to be enough:
the trying, and the tea going cold,
and Bill's laugh still somewhere
in the room's used air, and the sense—
however fragile, however hard-won—
that I am, despite everything,
still capable of being held.

# Zenithit: Ein faszinierendes Mineral

Zenithit ist der Name eines seltenen Minerals, das durch seine charakteristische Kristallstruktur und außergewöhnlichen optischen Eigenschaften auffällt. Der Name leitet sich vom lateinischen Wort "zenith" ab, was auf den höchsten Punkt oder Gipfel verweist – eine Anspielung auf die intensive Farbbrillanz und den besonderen Glanz des Minerals.

## Eigenschaften und Erscheinungsbild

Zenithit zeichnet sich durch eine tiefblaue bis violette Färbung aus, die je nach Lichteinfall changiert. Diese Farbwechsel entstehen durch mikroskopisch kleine Einschlüsse, die das einfallende Licht auf besondere Weise brechen. Die Kristalle bilden häufig prismatische Strukturen aus und erreichen eine bemerkenswerte Härte auf der Mohsschen Härteskala.

## Entstehung und Fundorte

Die Bildung dieses Minerals erfolgt typischerweise in hydrothermalen Adern unter spezifischen Druck- und Temperaturbedingungen. Solche geologischen Prozesse benötigen oft Millionen von Jahren, bis sich die charakteristischen Kristallformationen ausbilden.

## Bedeutung und Verwendung

Aufgrund seiner Seltenheit und ästhetischen Qualitäten wird Zenithit sowohl von Sammlern als auch in der Schmuckherstellung geschätzt. In esoterischen Kreisen wird dem Mineral zudem eine besondere energetische Wirkung zugeschrieben, wobei solche Zuschreibungen wissenschaftlich nicht belegt sind.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness free verse poem about waking up in the middle of the night, unable to sleep, and drifting into memories of a deceased poet friend.
counterfactuals.output:
**3 A.M., Thinking of You Again**

the clock says something I don't want to know
red numbers breathing in the dark like a small
patient animal and my mouth is dry
and the ceiling has that water stain shaped like
nothing, like a country that doesn't exist,
and I am awake the way a bruise is awake
under the skin, dull and insistent and blue

somewhere in this not-sleeping my mind walks
without asking me, down the hall of you—
your hands, always ink-stained, that blue-black
smudge on the side of your palm from writing
left to right, dragging the wet words with you,
you used to say a poem isn't finished
it's abandoned, and laugh that laugh that cracked
in the middle like a dropped glass

I keep doing the math of you, how many
years now, how many springs you haven't seen,
the cherry trees you loved so much have bloomed
without permission four times since you left
and nobody asked them to stop, the nerve
of the world, going on, unbothered,
the audacity of gardens

I remember you reading in that kitchen
with the yellow light, coffee gone cold,
saying *listen to this line* and I didn't
listen, not really, not the way I should have,
I was thinking about my own small worries,
some bill, some fight, some nothing,
and now I would give a year of nights like this
just to not listen to you again

the house makes its settling sounds, a creak
like something shifting its weight in another room,
and for a second, half-drowned in dark,
I let myself believe it's you
adjusting yourself in the doorway,
still curious about my insomnia,
still asking *what keeps you up, what keeps you*

nothing keeps me, that's the trouble,
there's no rope, no ledge, just this
falling that doesn't fall, just lying here
holding the shape of a person
who isn't a shape anymore, who is
weather now, who is the smell of rain
before rain, who is a line I can't
finish because you're the only one
who knew how it went

I get up for water I don't need
just to move through my body,
just to prove I still have one,
the floor is cold in that particular way
that reminds you you're alive, small
mercies, small stupid mercies

back in bed I say your name
once, quietly, an experiment,
to see what happens
nothing happens
the night keeps its silence
like a fist
and I lie here
folding and unfolding
the dark
like a letter
I already know by heart
and still
can't stop
rereading

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, dreamlike poem in the style of John Ashbery about domestic night routines, existential dread, and the death of a fellow writer named Bill.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ten O'Clock, and the House Begins Its Confession**

Someone has left the porch light on again, a small
insurrection against the larger dark, which doesn't mind,
having so much of itself to spare. I go around
checking the stove, though nothing was cooking, though
the idea of flame persists in the eye like a word
you've used too often to still hear.

Bill used to say the night was just the day
with its coat turned inside out, and now Bill
is a fact arranged differently than before,
a sentence that stopped choosing its next word.
I lock the door. I lock it again. The lock
agrees to keep agreeing, which is more
than can be said for the weather, or the heart,
which changes its mind the way a room changes
when you've left it and come back holding a glass
you don't remember filling.

Upstairs, the faucet completes its small argument
with silence and loses, the way we all do,
eventually, on the numbers. I brush my teeth
as if performing a rite whose god
retired years ago to a cabin upstate
and doesn't answer the phone, though the phone
keeps ringing in the house of the dead,
who are notoriously bad correspondents
but excellent listeners, Bill among them now,
his ear turned toward whatever we're saying
about him at dinner parties, which is less
than we mean and more than we intend.

The dark outside the window is doing
what dark does—filling in the shapes
of the maple, the fence, the neighbor's
inexplicable trampoline—with a patience
that would be admirable in a person.
I turn off the hall light. The house exhales.
Somewhere a version of tomorrow is already
practicing its excuses.

I think of Bill's unfinished manuscript,
how it sits now like a held breath
no one will release, how the last line
trails off not from despair but simply
because the hand that was writing it
had somewhere else to be, some appointment
none of us were told about, a meeting
already in progress before we knew
there was a room.

I check the door one more time.
It's not about safety. It's about the ritual
of touching the same cold handle
and finding it, against all evidence,
still there—the world's small mercy,
handed to us nightly, like a note
passed under a door we didn't know
was locked, that says: *not yet,
not yet, but soon, and in the meantime,
here is a house, here is a bed,
here is the dark you asked for,
arriving right on schedule,
carrying no one you have lost.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long-form confessional poem that mixes mundane details (kitchen, TV, lake) with cosmic imagery (radiation, waves, sky) and ends with an address to a dead friend's spirit.
counterfactuals.output:
**Static**

I.
The refrigerator hums its one dumb hymn
and I stand in its light at midnight
eating cold rice from the container,
thinking how every kitchen is a chapel
if you stay in it long enough alone.

There's a plate in the drying rack
shaped like the moon at three-quarters full.
I could tell you this is a coincidence.
I could tell you a lot of things.

The dish soap smells like fake lemons,
like something trying very hard to be alive.

II.
On the television, a man in a blue suit
explains the weather that has already happened.
I keep the sound off and watch his mouth
open and close like a fish
that thinks it's speaking to God.

Static, when the antenna slips,
is just old light—
photons that left their stars
before either of us had names,
arriving now, in my den,
dressed up as nothing,
as snow on a screen,
as the sound a universe makes
when it's tired of being empty.

III.
I drove to the lake because I didn't know
what else a body does with itself
on a Tuesday that refuses to end.

The water was the color of a bruise
healing wrong. Ducks moved across it
like punctuation in a sentence
no one will finish.

I thought: this is a wave.
I thought: so is light.
I thought: so, apparently, is grief—
it keeps arriving in the same place,
long after the thing that made it
has stopped touching the water.

IV.
They put you under a machine once
that hummed like the refrigerator,
like the low channel between stations,
and told you it was healing you
with something too small to see—
particles undoing particles,
the body its own quiet cosmos
being rearranged from the inside.

I sat in the waiting room
reading a magazine about kitchens,
about the best way to organize a drawer,
while somewhere down the hall
you were being irradiated
by the same kind of light
that still floats between galaxies,
looking for something to lean against.

V.
Isn't it strange—
we are made of the stuff
that stars threw off when they died,
and still we set the table,
still we argue about the remote,
still we forget to take the chicken out to thaw,
as if none of this matters against a sky
that doesn't even know we're watching it.

But the sky doesn't have to know.
That's what I keep learning, badly,
late, in kitchens, on shorelines,
in front of screens that hiss
with light too old to have a name.

VI.
So, Danny—
because I'm done pretending
this was ever a poem about anything else—

I don't know where you are,
if "where" even applies to you now,
if you've become some kind of frequency
too faint for my antenna,
some hush behind the static
I mistake for nothing.

I want to tell you the lake still does that thing
where the sun makes a road across it
like it's inviting someone to walk out.
I want to tell you I bought the same bad coffee
you used to make fun of.
I want to tell you the moon was three-quarters full
and looked exactly like a plate
someone forgot to put away.

If you're radiation now,
if you're some slow decay
lighting up a body that isn't a body,
then find the gap in my reception,
find the place where the picture goes to snow,
and sit there with me a minute,
the way we used to sit at the end of the dock
not talking, just watching the water
do what water does—

hold the sky without meaning to,
and let it go, and hold it again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# Static

The phone glows blue against my face like
a small moon I made myself, orbiting
nothing, and I keep

refreshing the space where your name used to
autocomplete. The algorithm doesn't know
you're gone. It suggests

I message you happy birthday. I almost
do. My thumb hovers the way grief
hovers, undecided,

over which door. There's a word for the specific
static between stations—I forget it
the way I forget

which of your sweaters I gave away, which
I kept, which one still holds the shape
of your shoulders

when I'm not looking. 3 a.m. and the servers
hum somewhere in a cold room, keeping
every message

we never
sent

alive. I used to think loneliness was
silence. Now I know it's this—the blue
light insisting

there's always someone
awake somewhere, always
a signal, always

a small red notification
that isn't
you.

The dead don't buffer. They don't
lag or reconnect. They just
stop,

mid-sentence,
like the last text you sent
that still says *delivered*

not
*read.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
